notes: Line forms: {n} Feyre's narration, first person past tense, shown in italics; {s,e,t} a line spoken aloud (speaker, portrait expression, text); {hint} a game tip on its own card; {choices:[{t,goto,do}]}; {do:[actions]}; {goto}. Any line or choice may carry if_flag, if_not_flag, if_item, if_not_item or if_chapter. Wording is written for the game; the few short book lines kept are listed in quotes.json.

lines.n: The floors gleamed from scrubbing, and windows had been thrown open just so the rose-scented air could drift in. All for me. As though I'd ever minded a little dust.

lines.t: Why do it? Why be so kind?
Nobody in this house has loved these things in a long time. It's good to see them put to use.

lines.n: And then I looked up at the paintings, and forgot to breathe.

So many, so different, and yet hung so that they flowed together. Pastorals, portraits, still lifes. Each one a voice, shouting or whispering or singing, crying out into the dark of time that someone had been here, had felt this.
Some were painted through eyes like mine. Others bent the world in ways no human eye could have, in colors I'd never imagined. And still I understood them, and felt them, and cared.

lines.t: I never knew humans could...

lines.n: He trailed off as I turned. My cheeks were wet. My heart was a fierce, grieving, humbled thing.

lines.t: Thank you.
Come here whenever you like.

lines.n: He left me to it. I stayed for hours, until I was drunk on it, dizzy with hunger.
After lunch, Alis led me to a bare room beyond the gallery. Canvases large and small. Brushes. And paints, far more colours than the four I'd dared to hope for.

do.text: Your painting room is through the gallery's east door.

lines.n: The room was quiet, and full of clear light, and waiting, and utterly mine.
I began to paint.
I started on him and gave up three times before noon. The gold of his mask was easy. What was under it was not.
Weeks went by, and the days melted together. Most of what I painted was awful. I never let anyone see it, however much Tamlin prodded or Lucien smirked at the paint on my clothes.

Some days I rode out with Tamlin to see his lands and came home with ideas that had me out of bed at dawn. Other days he was called to the borders and came back in blood that wasn't his. He never told me about it, and I never asked. That he came back was enough.

I still dreamed of the deaths I'd watched, and the ones I'd dealt, and of a pale woman pulling me to pieces while a shadow I could never make out looked on. But bit by bit, the fear let go of me. Keep to his side, the Suriel had said. So I did.
And then one morning, past the outer hedge, a warm wind blew up from the south. Spring was coming to the mortal lands.
My family, glamoured and fed and safe, didn't know where I was. Life had gone on without me. To them, I might as well have been in my grave. And he had let me stop thinking about them.

I didn't paint that day. I sat in front of a blank canvas with no colors in me at all. Maybe the paints had only ever been a way to keep me quiet. To stop me asking. And I had stopped, like a good, obedient human.
I made it through a tense dinner, and when it was over I went out into the dusk and lost myself among the hedges.

do.text: Walk it off in the rose garden.

lines.n: The low sun stained the red roses nearly purple and laid a sheen on the white ones.

lines.t: My father planted this garden for my mother. A gift, when they were mated.

lines.n: I didn't turn. I dug my nails into my palms. The flowers I had painted on our table at home were probably flaking away by now. Nesta might have scraped them off.

lines.t: You seem... upset.

lines.n: I tore a rose off the nearest bush. The thorns ripped my fingers and I didn't care.

lines.t: I don't know why I'm so ashamed of leaving them. Why it feels so selfish, so wicked, to paint. I know I shouldn't feel it. I can't help it.
All those years. And they didn't even try to stop you from taking me. I don't know why I believed the puca. I don't know why I still care.
Next to your borders, your magic, I suppose my self-pity is ridiculous.
If it grieves you, it isn't ridiculous at all.
Why?

lines.n: I flung the rose away into the hedge. He caught my hands, carefully, and raised my bleeding palm to his lips. Then the other one.
My knees nearly went. When he drew back, there was blood on his lips, and the cuts on my hands were gone.

lines.t: Don't feel bad for a moment about doing what brings you joy.

lines.n: He tucked the rose behind my ear. I hadn't seen him pick it up, and the thorns were gone.

lines.t: Why? Why do any of this?
Because the way mortals feel enchants me. You have so little time, and you feel everything in it so fiercely, all at once. It pulls at me, even when I know better. Even when I fight it.

lines.n: He leaned in slowly, leaving me every chance to step back, and his mouth grazed my cheek, light as a breath. I stayed where I was.

lines.t: Someday I'll answer every question you have. Just not yet. Not until it's safe.

lines.n: He left me there, and I let out the breath I hadn't known I was holding. I hadn't known how much I wanted him near until he was gone.
Mortified by everything I'd said, I slipped out to the woods after breakfast with my bow and Lucien's jeweled knife. Within the hour I felt someone following me, sending every bird for cover.
I smiled to myself. Twenty minutes later I was up an elm, waiting.
A snap, and a roar that scattered the birds. When I walked into the clearing, the High Lord of the Spring Court was hanging upside down by his ankles from my snare.

lines.t: Cruel human.
That's what you get for stalking people.

lines.n: I dared to run my fingers through his hair, hanging just above my face, all wheat and gold and brown. He leaned into my hand and purred. I felt it in my bones. I stepped back.
One claw through the vine, a flip, and he landed on his feet. Then he pulled three sheets of paper from his tunic.

lines.t: Before you bolt, or start shouting...

lines.n: Five short poems, full of words I didn't know. He read the first one over my shoulder, his breath on my ear: a lady most lovely, if a little unusual, with suitors lined up in a queue, and a refusal for every one of them.
The second was much less polite. By the third, my face was on fire.

lines.t: The last word of the second and fourth lines.

lines.n: Unusual. Queue. Slaying. Conflagration. My list.

lines.t: Your words were too interesting to waste, and useless for love poems. In my father's war-band we held contests for the filthiest rhymes. I don't like losing, so I got good at them.

lines.n: He read the fifth, the foulest of all. And I threw back my head and laughed, and it was like sun breaking through ice that had been there for years.

lines.t: You said your father planted the roses when they were mated. Not married?
Most of us marry. But if we're blessed, we find our mate. Our equal, our match in every way. If you find your mate, the bond runs so deep that marriage hardly matters.
What happened to your parents?

lines.n: His claws gleamed at his knuckles.

lines.t: My father was no better than Lucien's. He was worse, and my brothers with him. They owned slaves. I was only young when the Treaty was signed, but I remember the things my brothers did. When I saw you, and that house, I couldn't let myself turn into them.

My mother loved him too much to say a word against him. I never wanted his title. My brothers would have killed me if they'd thought I did. So I joined the war-band and trained, and found that fighting was about the only thing I was good at.
I doubt that.

I'm not bad with a fiddle. But a High Lord's son doesn't get to wander the roads playing for coins. My power kept growing until I couldn't hide it. Then a rival High Lord killed them all. I grieved for my mother. The others would never have lifted a finger to spare me what happened to you.
Most High Lords are bred for it: etiquette, law, court intrigue. When the title landed on me, half my father's courtiers walked out rather than bow to a soldier with claws.
Then they're idiots. You've kept these lands safe from the blight when others haven't.

lines.n: A shadow passed behind his eyes, and his shoulders curled in, a little.
On the hills beyond the woods, masked faeries were stacking great unlit fires.

lines.t: Bonfires. For Calanmai, Fire Night. Two days from now. We light the fires, and the magic we make renews the land for the year. There's a ritual. It's... very faerie.
Am I invited?
No. You're not.

lines.n: My chest caved a little. We walked back in a silence we hadn't had in weeks.
The moment we reached the gardens, he went rigid. Everything was quiet, with that terrible stillness that meant something foul was near.

lines.t: Hide. Whatever you hear, don't come out.

lines.hint: Get behind one of the hedges on the garden's north side before it comes, and keep still while it's near. Moving makes the gravel talk.

lines.n: A boom of leathery wings, a foul wind across my face, and everything went silent. Then huge hands closed on my shoulders, and I yelped.

lines.t: It's gone.
What did you hear?
Nothing I understood. What was that?
There are faeries in Prythian who gave you humans your worst stories. Some, like that one, are the stories given flesh.

lines.n: In that hissing voice I had heard screaming. Victims. Altars. And a court that wasn't his, and a she who commanded such a thing as her messenger.

lines.t: If the Attor saw her-
It didn't. I'll see you at dinner, Feyre.

lines.n: I'd been sent away. I went back to the house and bolted my door, and the spring wind murmured that I'd be happier not knowing who she was.
